newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Sasko milling co-op goes private.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Sasko milling co-op goes private.

text.p: The Sasko milling cooperative has converted to a private company and intends to seek a listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange to finance diversification, officials said on Friday.

The transition was sanctioned by 97 percent of the former cooperative's members at a special meeting in November and the new company was registered on Wednesday, group director of legal services Pieter Stoffberg told Reuters.

He said the company was registered as Saskor Foods (Pty) Ltd, but would change its name to Saskor (Pty) Ltd as soon as the name is relinquished by another of the group's companies, which is being deregistered.
A company spokeswoman said Saskor Foods held assets, mainly storage, milling and baking facilities, valued at 737 million rand.
She said turnover was 1.9 billion rand with a net profit after tax of 50 million rand in the financial year to September 30, 1995. More recent figures were not immediately available.
Group managing director Stephan Bellingan said the conversion would partially unlock value for members.

"Under a cooperative dispensation, members could only indicate the value of their shares in Sasko at a nominal value of two rand each, as opposed to the current net asset value of 240 rand a share," he said.
"The group is actively investigating risk-spreading diversification opportunities. Such a process could well lead to...eventual listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange."
Stoffberg said the conversion to a private company would put Sasko squarely into the market alongside other millers, but would not entail any preferential relationship with farmers.
He said Saskor would seek related diversification opportunities and would finance them through a listing.
"The plan is to list eventually, but if we do, it will be for the right reasons and not just for the sake of it. There will be a sound financial reason for it.
"We're in the market for acquisitions, but we will remain in food," he said.

Stoffberg said the conversation was unlikely to attract the government resistance that has faced KWV Investments Ltd's plan to become a private company because Sasko does not have and has not had any regulatory role in the industry.
He acknowledged, however, that the shareholders had built up an asset base under favourable tax conditions under apartheid.

The privatisation of assets accumulated under apartheid, when black farmers were virtually totally excluded from commercial agriculture, has attracted considerable opposition from the ruling African National Congress.
